questions_asked: In early 2023, did the daily pool of Wordle players post scores on Twitter at a steady rate, or did that rate drop over time as the game got old?
When a Wordle word has no repeated letters, can the standard yellow/green feedback still mislead players into thinking a shown letter is absent?
If you predicted the Wordle score share for a new word, how big an error band would make that estimate useless for the New York Times?
expert_answers: The rate was not steady — it declined over the year. Reported-result counts in the 2022 file are highest in the early months (roughly the first quarter) and trend downward through the year, with a clear decay plus strong day-of-week and word-difficulty effects. This is an empirical judgment from the data's overall shape, not a precise figure: expect a substantial drop from early-2022 peaks to late-2022 levels, on the order of tens of percent, not a flat line.

No. With no repeated letters, the standard feedback is unambiguous: each letter appears at most once in the solution, so a gray tile always means that letter is genuinely absent, and yellow/green always mean it is present. Misleading "absent" impressions arise only with repeated letters — e.g., a guess containing a letter twice when the solution has it once can show one gray tile for that letter, which players may misread as the letter being absent even though another copy is yellow/green.

An error band of roughly ±10 percentage points or more on any single score share (1–6, X) would make the estimate useless to the Times. At that width, the predicted distribution no longer distinguishes an easy word from a hard one — the whole point of the analysis — and the intervals for adjacent categories overlap so heavily that no actionable statement can be made.

For context, the actual day-to-day spread in these shares is itself only on the order of a few to ~10 points across categories, so a band that large would swamp the signal. A band of a few points (say ±2–3) is still informative; ±10 is not. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise threshold.
